text: State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk film. Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children. Veteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0. The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us: Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers. text: Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes. Oil price rises above $100 a barrel as Tehran responds to US attacks that sunk five Iranian tankers. Tehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two countries sent the oil price above $100 a barrel for the first time since July. The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports. The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark, is likely to raise inflation and the price of goods. Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis. Among the vessels struck by Iran were two US vessels and eight oil tankers, the Iranian’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Wednesday. The IRGC said the 10 vessels were “noncompliant” – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing. The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”. A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. text: Republicans kick off ‘midterm convention’ to overcome Trump unpopularity. GOP plans to center the president at rare two-day Texas event as party hopes to retain control of House in midterms. Republicans are gathering in Texas on Wednesday for a rare “midterm convention”, as they attempt to convince Americans to vote for a party led by a deeply unpopular president who has overseen inflation and led the US into an increasingly unpopular war. Donald Trump will dominate the two-day convention, appearing both nights as the GOP works to cling to control of the House of Representatives in November. Republicans plan to put the president at the center of the event, a bold strategy given his approval rating is hovering at about 38%, while accusing the Democratic party of being socialist and out of touch with Americans. However, in a sign of Trump’s toxicity, some vulnerable Republicans have said they will not attend the Dallas event: risking the potential ire of the president, but avoiding a public association with a deeply unpopular leader. Less than two months out from the midterm elections, the Republican party faces a serious battle to retain its slender control of the House, while Democrats are increasingly hopeful they could pick up Senate seats. Winning either would put the Democratic party in position to stymie Trump’s aims during his final two years in office. The convention represents perhaps Republicans’ final opportunity to make a large-scale, high-profile pitch to Americans. Joe Gruters, the chair of the Republican National Committee (RNC), which is organizing the convention, said the program would attempt to demonstrate how Republicans are “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Whether voters buy that is a different matter, given costs, including gas prices, have risen during Trump’s presidency. Forecasters give Republicans a slim chance of holding on to the House, in particular, and some members of Congress have been keen to distance themselves from the event. text: The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity. Editorial: The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel bills. Imperialism does not require a flag to be planted or a governor dispatched. It can be a powerful nation deciding who governs a smaller, weaker country, and on what terms and for whose benefit its resources will be developed. Donald Trump’s kidnapping of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, putting his deputy – Delcy Rodríguez – in his place as president, and then her signing a deal handing a fifth of the country’s proven oil reserves to the US, amount to a modern version of 19th-century gunboat diplomacy. Regime change supplied America’s commercial concession. This won’t bother Mr Trump. But it should. The US president has oversold his neocolonial spoils. The additional production Venezuela is supposed to bring online might bring down oil prices eventually, but not anytime soon. Crucially, what Mr Trump calls “the biggest oil deal in history” won’t cause the price at the pump to fall before November’s midterms. When so many American voters are struggling to pay energy bills, it’s hard to see how unrealised Orinoco Belt riches are going to help Republican candidates. The US president also promotes the idea that he is transforming the US’s industrial landscape through fossil fuels. text: Bond market rebuffs US treasury’s plan to buy back $6bn in government debt. Scott Bessent made announcement on Wednesday as bond yields rose to highest point since 2008 financial crisis. The US treasury moved to cut the cost of borrowing on Wednesday only to be swiftly rebuffed by the bond market. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, announced the US would buy back $6bn worth of government debt – treasuries – in an effort to alleviate a selloff in the US bond market that has put pressure on interest rates. But the size of the deal failed to appease bond buyers and the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high. Rising inflation and uncertainty from the war in Iran have spooked investors from US bonds, historically known to be one of the safest investment vehicles. Treasury yields have been rising, with the yield for the 30-year treasury bond hitting about 5.2% – the highest yield since the 2008 financial crisis. In an attempt to alleviate the bond market, Bessent on 19 August announced the treasury would at least double its typical buyback operation. The move is meant to stabilize the market: fewer bonds on the market should mean that yields go down. But in the weeks since the announcement, treasury yields have continued to rise. Even after Bessent announced the operation would target $6bn worth of government bonds, yields on Wednesday continued to rise. In August, US government debt for the first time in the country’s history reached $40tn – double the amount of debt from just 10 years ago. text: Ryanair boss says airline will dispute account of passenger who said they were partially sucked out of window – as it happened. Ljubisa Karović suffered neck and shoulder injuries after the window broke during the flight. Ryanair has said it will be “disputing” that any part of a passenger’s body was sucked outside when a window on one of its aircraft broke while in flight. US investigators are examining the incident which left Ljubisa Karović, 61, severely injured when the window beside him shattered on a Ryanair flight from Greece to Germany in July. Karović’s lawyer said the Serbian businessman was hauled back in after his head and right arm were sucked through the window due to the sudden depressurisation. However, Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said the airline would be “disputing” that account, telling reporters after the airline’s annual meeting in Dublin on Thursday that Karović was “certainly sucked towards the window, but he didn’t get out the window”. The European Central Bank raised interest rates by a quarter point, the second hike this year, seeking to tame an energy-driven rise in inflation triggered by the Iran war, as it warned that fuel prices could move higher. A relative lull in the conflict came to an end in recent weeks, and in recent days the US and Iran hit ⁠military, shipping and energy assets, sending oil ⁠back above $100 a barrel – now at $104.53 a barrel, but approached $106 a barrel earlier. Natural gas prices have also jumped today. The ECB responded by raising its policy rate to 2.50% from 2.25%. It acknowledged that even then inflation is expected to stay above the central bank’s 2% target through to 2028, in part ⁠because activity in the wider economy is more resilient than thought. The ECB decision and statement prompted traders to raise bets on further hikes, pricing in 60 basis points more of increases by the April 2027 meeting, up from around 51 bps before. As usual, ECB president Christine Lagarde stressed the ⁠bank does not pre-commit to any future moves. She told a press conference We have not debated at all any kind of future path. Markets do what they have to do and we do what we have to do - which is to provide price stability.

text: Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’. Critics react to bid for Republican votes with incredulity and point to potential $1.2tn cost atop existing national debt. Donald Trump’s promise of a $5,000 “Trump dividend” for every US citizen if Republicans retain control of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has sparked incredulity and accusations of bribery. “If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said during the unprecedented Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump dividend.” It comes amid extreme concern over the US national debt, which exceeded $40tn for the first time in August. Speaking to Politico, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, sounded skeptical. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said. In the moments after Trump made the announcement, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X that “this would cost about $1.2 TRILLION in just one year. That’s more than ALL THREE ROUNDS of COVID relief checks, despite no recessions. The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.” The US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting the cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt. “The 10-year [treasury bond is] approaching 5%,” Goldwein said on Thursday morning. “Inflation is not under control. We spend more on interest than we spend on defense or on Medicare at this point. Social security is six years from insolvency. Just about the last thing we need is to borrow another trillion dollars to send checks to everybody.” Spending like this risked an economic sugar high followed by a recessionary crash, he said. But Goldwein was most concerned about what might happen if Trump’s gambit is effective. “If this works, the lesson for every future politician is going to be: if you want to win an election, promise a trillion dollars. And multiply a trillion dollars times the number of elections we have coming up, that is a recipe for bankruptcy.”

text: Does Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ count as a bribe if we never get the money? . Trump’s promise to pay $5,000 to every adult US citizen if the Republicans win in November was only one questionable moment in a nearly two-hour speech. Hello, from the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, where on Wednesday night Trump definitely, definitely, did not try to bribe the American public into voting for his party in November. Speaking for almost two hours at the American Airlines Center, Trump promised to pay every adult citizen in the US $5,000 if Republicans retain the House and Senate in the midterm elections. The speech felt very much like a desperate last pitch to voters: the electoral equivalent of a dumped boyfriend offering to take his estranged girlfriend on a mini-break to Venice. It’s very important that even if the $5,000 offer might sound like a bribe – “if you do this for me, I will give you this money” – it is not a bribe; instead serving as a “dividend”, paid because of what Trump says is his administration’s “tremendous economic success”. The $5,000 non-bribe – inducement, perhaps – was the headline of Trump’s speech, during which the president was the liveliest he’s appeared in months. There were no surreptitious naps here as Trump rattled through some of his greatest hits (Sleepy Joe, Barack Hussein, Crooked Hillary) to the delight, initially, of the crowd. I say “initially” because this was evidence that you can have too much of a good thing. Even your favorite entertainer can go on too long. That was the case here, as an arena that wasn’t even full to begin with began to quietly empty after an hour and a half as Trump, becoming visibly drained by this point, leaned on his lectern and called Democrats “communist” for the 11th time. Nervous investors across big economies have been dumping government bonds, driving up the cost of borrowing, as surging oil prices amplified fears about rising inflation. The cost of a barrel of oil jumped 6% to above $107 on Thursday amid concerns that advances by Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast in Yemen could choke off Saudi crude exports. The global bond sell-off that has rocked markets in recent weeks resumed in response to the news from the Middle East – which came against a backdrop of escalating concern about out-of-control government borrowing. Higher oil prices, which had already climbed since hostilities resumed in the Iran war, are expected to drive up inflation, prompting central banks to raise interest rates and putting the brakes on economic growth. Donald Trump suggested on Wednesday that the conflict with Iran could continue until “immediately after” November’s US midterm elections, at which point he claimed oil prices would be “tumbling downward”. text: ‘I’m on the ticket’: Trump implores Republicans to vote in November at unusual midterm convention. The president demonised Democrats in an attempt to wangle votes in midterms despite backlash over Iran war. With his approval rating at a historic low, Donald Trump has brought down the curtain on the Republicans’ first ever midterm convention by pleading with supporters to do him “the biggest favour” and “pretend” they are voting for him in November’s US elections. The president is facing a growing backlash over rising prices and the war in Iran. Sweeping losses for the Republican party could effectively turn Trump into a lame duck for his final two years in the White House. Sensing political danger, Trump wrapped up the novel two-day event in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday with a pitch that critics are likely to say smacked of desperation: “You gotta do me the biggest favour you’ve ever done me. You’ve gotta do this for me. You’ve got to pretend I’m on the ticket. I’m on the ticket! I’m on the ticket! He’s on the ticket! Pretend I’m on the ticket because this is going to turn out to be one of the most important elections.” In an improvised pledge of allegiance to himself, Trump directed the crowd of about 20,000 to raise their right hands and repeat: “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States, that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends, I’ll do it any way – I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try to cheat like hell like they do.” The convention had been aimed at turning around Republicans’ fortunes. Opinion polls suggest they are on course to lose the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate. In what was effectively an abridged version of his rambling keynote address on Wednesday, the president reiterated his promise of “Trump dividend” of $5,000 for every US adult if Republicans win both chambers of Congress. Democrats have dismissed the pledge as a bribe while economists have warned it would cost more than $1tn. Trump also hammered the theme of the convention: drawing a contrast between his own accomplishments and what he argues amounts to a threat posed by Democrats.

text: Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfold. The world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home. As clear as that cloudless September morning, Jenna Jacobs McPartland remembers the moment everything changed. “I was cleaning the bathroom and watching the Today show in the background and nine months pregnant,” the 52-year-old recalls by phone. “I think they were showing ‘Today throws a wedding’ when the news broke in.” A plane had hit the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. McPartland did not know that her husband, Ariel Jacobs, was attending a conference at its Windows on the World restaurant. “I called his office to say, ‘Hey, turn on the TV. Do you guys know what’s going on?’ His assistant said, ‘Oh my God, Jenna, he’s there.’ The whole world disappeared and there was this sort of hollow collapsing feeling.” Ariel Jacobs did not live to see his son, Gabriel, born six days after September 11, 2001. text: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’. Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise. Fuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil price to its highest since mid-May. As investors dumped stocks and bonds in an increasingly febrile environment, Donald Trump’s promise to give every US adult citizen a US$5,000 “dividend” after the November midterms if Republicans win added to alarm around the parlous state of the country’s finances. Investors pushed US bond yields towards 5% for the first time since 2007 as the prospect of higher energy costs firmed up expectations that the US Federal Reserve would need to hike rates again. That dragged Australia’s 10-year rate up to 5.38% and to fresh 15-year highs. The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed towards US$110 a barrel, before settling at above US$108 in late Friday trade. Steve Miller, an investment strategist at fund manager GSFM, said bonds were reacting to a “deadly cocktail” of high oil prices, American fiscal irresponsibility, and worries around the independence of the Fed. “The $5,000 promise is a great example of Trump’s unwillingness to tackle the deficit, and even to make it worse for short-term political expediency. No wonder bond markets are sketchy,” Miller said. Tai Hui, chief market strategist for Asia-Pacific at JP Morgan Asset Management, said rising long-term borrowing rates would normally undermine stock valuations, as investors rethink the relative trade-off between the riskier sharemarket and climbing yields on safe bonds. text: First Thing: Nation pauses to remember September 11 on 25th anniversary. Commemoration ceremonies to be held around the world for the nearly 3,000 killed in 2001 terror attack on US. Plus, JD Vance sets out his stall as heir to Donald Trump. Good morning. It is a sombre day for the nation as people gather to mourn and remember the nearly 3,000 victims of the attacks on September 11 2001, when 19 al-Qaida hijackers seized control of four airliners, slamming two of the planes into the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth into a field in western Pennsylvania. We have comprehensive coverage of the anniversary, which will be marked by ceremonies around the world. There are stories of the day from people who were there. Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark were two of only four individuals known to have survived above the impact zone in the south tower, and they spoke to our Washington bureau chief David Smith. Anna Sweeney Rossman was five when her mother, Amy Sweeney, a flight attendant, was killed onboard American Airlines flight 11, and she spoke to Ramon Antonio Vargas about how the events of that day have cast a shadow on her life. CIA veterans spoke to Robert Tait about the chaos and confusion in the agency as the unprecedented attacks unfolded, and Guardian readers have told us about how September 11 changed their lives. Jason Burke, our international security correspondent, writes that while al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden may have shaken the world on 9/11, it is clear today his wider plans failed. But we also have to acknowledge that the world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home. This read from David Smith outlines how the day saw heroes emerge showing the best of America, and then the response of US governments left a dark legacy – Guantánamo Bay, the Abu Ghraib scandal – which continues to unfold to this day. Those who remember September 11 will never forget the haunting images of that day, including the missing people posters that were put up in the confusing aftermath of the collapse of the towers in New York. Captured by the photographer Phil Buehle

text: Wake up, Britain: Donald Trump’s US is no friend of ours. We must secure our own place in the world . The US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t wait, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins. If Americans vote for a Republican majority in both houses of Congress in November, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.” But they must not spend it in Canada or China or anywhere else outside the US. So said Donald Trump in Texas on Wednesday in advance of the forthcoming midterm elections. He further told voters to “Pretend that I’m on the ballot”. It was a climactic moment in an almost two-hour rant. Trump does not have the required trillion dollars in his pocket, and it would be illegal to disperse such a sum without congressional approval. In any case, JD Vance now appears to have rowed back on the promise. Observers from abroad must beware: it is unwise to subject Trump’s populism to the discipline of truth. Trump also said Americans should thank him for attacking Iran since that country was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”, which it intended to use against them. It was the old Saddam Hussein gambit. The problem is that almost every one of Trump’s speeches refers back to himself, as if he and the United States were synonymous. He claimed to have won the presidency three times. He says: “If we hadn’t won the last election, I’m not sure that our country right now would even exist.” He added that the arena where he was speaking was packed, with crowds outside clamouring to get in. text: US consumers faced more high prices in August as Iran war raised energy costs. Annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, same as July, and core inflation, which omits energy and food prices, rose to 2.4%. US consumer prices remained stubbornly high in August as the end of the ceasefire between the US and Iran pushed energy prices up, according to data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Friday. The annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, the same as it was in July. The most recent peak was seen in May, when the inflation rate hit a three-year high at 4.2%. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, increased 0.3% from the month before and 2.4% annually. Gasoline increased 27.4% compared with the year before, accounting for more than one-third of the overall monthly increase in prices. Fuel , which is used to power and heat homes, increased annually at a staggering 52%. Prices of common grocery store essentials, such as meat, poultry, eggs and dairy, increased slightly, from 0.1% to 0.3%. Lettuce prices continued to fall, probably continued fallout from the cyclosporiasis outbreak. Despite dipping from its most recent peak, inflation remained above levels that were seen before the war in Iran, largely because of higher energy prices. On Friday, the cost of diesel, used for trucks, buses and trains, rose past $6 a gallon for the first time ever. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, also surpassed $108 on Friday, its highest level since May. text: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s midterm convention: ‘That arena was as empty as a Waymo’. Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s ‘promise’ to send $5,000 to every US adult should the Republicans win. Late-night hosts recapped the second day of Donald Trump’s underattended and unusual “midterm convention” in which he promised $5,000 for every adult US citizen if the Republicans win. Jimmy Kimmel Jimmy Kimmel opened Thursday’s monologue with a report from the second day of the Republican National Committee’s “midterm convention” in Dallas, held at the request of Donald Trump. “He demanded a midterm convention, which is something that had never been done before, because there’s no reason to do that,” Kimmel explained. “And of course he got it. They do whatever he wants.” Trump spent the previous night posting on Truth Social, disputing all evidence that the Dallas arena was less than crowded. “He is so embarrassingly desperate to convince us that the place was packed. At the Republicans’ midterm convention held earlier this week, Donald Trump said that “food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down”. Fresh inflation data on Friday told a different story – but in one specific case, costs have been chopped. The price of lettuce dropped dramatically this summer after the cyclospora outbreak caused demand to wilt, with prices dropping even further in August, according to new data released on Friday. The crop was closely linked to the diarrhea-causing parasite that has seen more than 19,500 confirmed cases in the US since May – 16 times the cases that were seen in the same period in 2025. The outbreak spread to 20 states, with just more than 1,000 hospitalizations and two deaths, according to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Prices had already gone down 16.4% the month prior, the largest decrease in recent history. The economics behind food prices are often a mixed bag, but experts say there is a strong connection between lower lettuce prices and the cyclospora outbreak. text: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see unified Ireland and ‘it may as well happen now’ as he visits Dublin – as it happened. US president is meeting politicians and business leaders – and playing golf – during two-day trip to Ireland. That’s all from us on the US politics blog, thanks for following along. Here is a recap of the day’s developments: While in Ireland for a two-day visit that combined political meetings with a stop at his Doonbeg golf resort, Donald Trump said he backed Irish reunification. He said he would “love to see” a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”. He added that unification would happen eventually and suggested it would be “fantastic”. His comments prompted a backlash from unionists and UK politicians. Andy Burnham’s position on Irish unification remains unchanged, a spokesperson for the prime minister said. Earlier this week, Burnham said he would stick to the Good Friday agreement “100%” and that there would be no referendum without majority public support. Similarly, Micheál Martin’s government said Trump’s comments would not change its position, with a spokesperson saying it was committed to the Good Friday agreement and programme for government. text: Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears. Project will prepare volunteers across US to monitor polls, encourage early voting and respond to disinformation. The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies. The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation. The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races. These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Thirty state parties have a trained election protection director, with the goal of all states having one in place. The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant. The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process. text: Disaster insurance, datacenters, right to repair: meet the midterm candidates running on green policies. Some of the everyday struggles animating voters have a climate link lurking in the background. When Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a law erasing the words “climate change” from state statutes in May 2024 – colloquially known as the “don’t say climate change” law – Democrats were outraged. Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. After Donald Trump won the 2024 election, mentions of the climate crisis started to disappear from Democrats’ rhetoric. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail. The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations. The climate crisis, however, is still rearing its head around the country, fueling the heatwaves, wildfires and floods plaguing communities around the US. It also lurks behind issues animating voters, from datacenter expansion to rising home insurance rates. text: DHS officers raise concerns over potentially illegal voter searches and unreliable data, whistleblower says. Officers were instructed to search state voter databases and create federal records on suspected non-citizen voters despite concerns over the process. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating voter fraud they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information, an anonymous whistleblower revealed on Monday. DHS officers also had concerns about the reliability of the data they were working with, the whistleblower said. The Trump administration has ramped up its investigation into noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare and the effort has only turned up a handful of cases so far. As part of the effort, officers tasked with investigating potential non-citizen voters were told to take data DHS had compiled on voters and run it through state websites where voters can look up their voter information. Some states require voters to click attestations affirming that they are looking up their own voter information. On the Virginia Department of Elections website, for example, voters must click a disclaimer that says: “I certify and affirm that the information provided to access my voter registration is my own or I am expressly authorized by the voter to access this information. Gavin Newsom, the California governor, will not run for president if former vice-president Kamala Harris does, he said in a forthcoming interview with CNN. text: First Thing: States given clearance for mail-in voting as US supreme court thwarts Trump. Civil rights groups have praised verdict on administration’s last-ditch attempt to change midterm voting processes. Good morning. The supreme court has rejected Donald Trump’s mail ballot restrictions, capping a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting in the midterm elections already under way. The decision allows states to continue sending out mail ballots under the same processes they have used for years. Civil rights groups lauded the decision. “The supreme court has done the right thing,” said Robert Garcia, a Democratic representative from Long Beach, California, adding: “Donald Trump tried to illegally interfere with our elections and undermine vote-by-mail for millions of Americans and failed. We will keep fighting to protect the right to vote of every single citizen in this country.” What has a DHS whistleblower said about “voter fraud” investigations? An anonymous whistleblower said Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating “voter fraud” they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information. The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review, as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. Under the code of conduct, Microsoft’s AI models must not consider requests related to weapons development, produce violent or sexually explicit content or help with the procurement of dangerous substances. text: US treasury secretary hails government’s bond buyback a success. On Tuesday, the 10-year treasury rate yield reached a 19-year high at 5.041% as investors are wary Iran war fallout. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, claimed the government’s massive buyback of US bonds was a success. The claim came as the 10-year treasury yield reached a 19-year high on Tuesday, increasing pressure on interest rates as the Federal Reserve weighs another hike to see off rising inflation. US treasury yields, or the rate of return that investors receive when a bond matures, underpin the rates of other loans such as mortgages, car payments and credit card debt. On Tuesday, the yield rate for the 10-year treasury reached 5.041%, the highest level since 2007. The treasury yield rises when demand for bonds goes down. Though the US bond market is typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, investors have been wary of the effect the war in Iran is having on energy prices. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, hit $108 a barrel last week for the first time since May. When bond yields started to rise in August, the US treasury announced it would triple its buyback of government debt, going from $2bn to $6bn in an effort to bring down bond yields. Though the yields have continued to rise since, Bessent told Congress on Tuesday the operations are “the two most successful treasury auctions that we’ve had in 20 years”. “Since President Trump has come in, [the US bond market] has been the best-performing bond market in the developing world,” Bessent said. text: Republican Thomas Massie proposes impeaching Pete Hegseth over Iran war. Congressman says defense secretary repeatedly violated constitution through his handling of Iran war. The Republican congressman Thomas Massie on Tuesday proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide. The proposal by Massie, an iconoclastic lawmaker who lost his primary earlier this year after Donald Trump and Hegseth urged voters to oppose him, may put House Republicans in a bind just weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, in which they are defending their control of Congress. The final tally of 220-204 was similar to earlier votes, with a few more Republicans joining most Democrats in calling for an end to the war. But the comment that ricocheted across the internet – a clip of just a few seconds – was an almost-throwaway reference about how the US president wants to “travel with Natalie” onboard Air Force One. The crowd cheered the US senator, who is running for re-election in battleground Georgia and is increasingly seen as a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028. But his target audience that day – and this year – spanned far beyond the concert hall. As the US war with Iran drags on, the ranks of Republicans signaling the conflict is a liability for their party continues to grow. When the House of Representatives on Tuesday evening considered its sixth war powers resolution intended to force Donald Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict, three Republicans who had not supported the previous efforts broke with their party to vote this one to passage. Earlier that day, a Republican who had lost his primary after repeatedly clashing with Trump proposed impeaching the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, alleging a variety of constitutional transgressions including prosecuting the war against Iran without congressional authorization. The rebellions in the GOP are thus far mostly symbolic – Trump has ignored the sole war powers resolution to make it through both the House and Senate, and the prospects of Hegseth’s impeachment are unclear. text: > The trouble for the US is that it is now very clear that the US president can just act like a crazy dictator, and that the mechanisms which were supposed to prevent that simply don't function. This is true. A US president who has strong support from a majority of voters of his own party can act like a dictator. So if 51% of Republican voters (which may be just 25% of all voters) support him no matter what, then he can act like a dictator. This is because Republican members of Congress who are supposed to rein him in are worried that they will be voted out if they anger the 25% of voters who support the president. The fact that 25% of voters can set the direction for the whole country is indeed a defect in the system that is not easily rectified. But if Republicans are defeated by Democrats in the upcoming midterms then there is hope. That's how we are going to recover.

text: ‘Inflation is too high and has been for too long,’ says Kevin Warsh as Fed announces rate hikes – as it happened. This live blog is now closed.. The US Federal Reserve voted unanimously to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, in a decision that marks chair Kevin Warsh’s first major step to try to tamp down inflation. The Fed’s open market committee voted 12-0 to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a new range of 3.75% to 4%, potentially setting Warsh on a collision course with Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed for rates to be cut and nominated Warsh with that expectation. Warsh, who assumed the role in May, said the Fed had concluded that “the plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Although Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, he avoided calling out the US-Israel war against Iran by name. He also declined to provide an indication of whether or not this hike will be the first in a series of increases, as has typically happened in the past. Warsh also declined to comment on Trump’s demands and threats and how he might react, asserting that Fed’s independence means: “We stay in our lane.” We’ve yet to hear from Donald Trump on what he makes of the news, but no doubt we will soon. text: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel. Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs. The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock to one of the largest US arms transfers of Trump’s second term, refusing to clear a $2.8bn sale of 2,000lb bombs to Israel. Gregory Meeks announced the hold on Tuesday on a package of 40,000 of the bombs, among the most destructive conventional munitions in the US arsenal. “The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” he said. “I therefore will not clear this sale at this time.” The deal, funded through US Foreign Military Financing, covers 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads. Meeks cannot single-handedly veto the $2.8bn arms transfer, but his leverage comes from the informal custom of “tiered review”. Under this practice, the state department submits major weapons packages to top foreign affairs lawmakers for an informal sign-off before triggering a formal notification to Congress. Killing the sale outright would need a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, a bar Congress has not cleared. A similar push by the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders failed along party lines in April. In 2025, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, declared a national security emergency to bypass congressional review and fast-track nearly $3bn in weapons, including more than 35,000 heavy bombs and 4,000 bunker-buster warheads. text: The (vast?) majority of the debt happened as the result of the Republican party both increasing spending and cutting taxes every time it lands someone in the White House and before midterms flip the House back to Democrats. There's a fair argument to be made that the Democrats could/should have reversed these disastrous fiscal policies when they gained power, but it's important to be wary of Murc's Law while also acknowledging doing so would also burn a lot of political capital Democrats never seem to have much of. The American electorate is a grade school child constantly evaluating which parent it likes the most. One tells you that you can eat as much candy as you like and play video games all night (neither of which hit you until the following day), while the other occasionally tells you to eat your vegetables, do your homework, and clean your room.

The American electorate is a grade school child constantly evaluating which parent it likes the most. One tells you that you can eat as much candy as you like and play video games all night (neither of which hit you until the following day), while the other occasionally tells you to eat your vegetables, do your homework, and clean your room.

text: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers. Act divides Democrats and Republicans, with some saying it gives president power that could be turned against US allies. The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago. The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results. However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead. The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports. text: US has some of the world's largest natural gas deposits, and is a major producer of helium, so it makes less sense to have a strategic helium reserve. Even the SPR was created in the aftermath of the last middle east oil crisis, back when the US was a major net importer of oil, and many people have been saying we should scrap the SPR, as no major oil producer has an SPR. The problem with the SPR is that it is used to manipulate prices, which was why Biden on the one hand cut oil leases and reduced domestic oil production, but then did major SPR drawdowns before the election to hide the realities of these policies. Now Trump is playing the same game, sanctioning oil producers and creating wars in the middle east, but using the SPR to hide the effects of these policies until after the midterm. In both cases, we'd probably be better off without an SPR, so all of these actions against oil production would be immediately felt at the pump before the election and voters could respond quickly. It's just too tempting to have this tool to manipulate oil prices that incumbents can use before elections.

text: Bad news this week for Trump – but Fox viewers might have missed it. The network continues to cater to its presidential ‘audience of one’, downplaying his supreme court loss and more. Two breaking stories roiled US politics this week and immediately got big play on most news sites. The supreme court surprisingly rejected – for now – Donald Trump’s attempted restrictions on mail-in ballots, a blow to Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. And the investigative site ProPublica revealed that a Russian oligarch had helped to bankroll the Bahamas wedding of Trump’s son Donald Jr, to the tune of hundreds of thousands of dollars. The blockbuster story quickly became ProPublica’s most-read article this year and was covered heavily elsewhere. “There’s no looking away from this Trump scoop,” wrote CNN’s Brian Stelter. Unless you watched Fox News, of course. There, it was business as usual. The wedding blockbuster got barely a nod on Monday night: a mere minute on the rightwing network’s evening programming, as the progressive non-profit watchdog Media Matters reported. It was much the same for the vote-by-mail story. “The news broke during the 7 p.m. hour, but Laura Ingraham, a law school grad, didn’t bother to tell viewers,” Stelter noted. Neither did the other big-name Fox opinion hosts, Jesse Watters and Sean Hannity. You would have had to wait until 11.30pm for that 45-second report, Stelter wrote, even as it was a leading story in many other places. In subsequent days, Fox paid more attention to both stories, but mostly to hand the megaphone to Trump’s trashing of the justices who didn’t give him what he demanded. Fox News has long billed itself as the more balanced alternative to mainstream media, an antidote to what Trump constantly slams as “fake news”. But in fact, the network often looks the other way when news comes along that might disturb its viewers, who still number in the millions during primetime hours. “This is the ‘negative space’ of Fox News coverage, in which they pretend something is simply not happening,” Matt Gertz, who tracks Fox News at Media Matters, told me. “Trumpian corruption is the biggest part of this,” Gertz said.

text: House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policies. María Elvira Salazar says some enforcement has ‘gone too far’ as GOP seeks distance from Trump before midterms. A Republican congresswoman has released a campaign ad criticizing Donald Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement, in the latest sign that a key plank of the president’s 2024 re-election campaign has become a liability for his congressional allies ahead of November’s midterm elections. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Florida’s María Elvira Salazar says in a 30-second ad. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” Salazar represents a competitive Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, and where Trump won by a 15-point margin two years ago after a campaign in which he promised to carry out “mass deportations”. While his administration has implied that those targeted would be undocumented immigrants who committed crimes in the United States, in reality, a substantial portion of the people arrested since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 have no criminal record. Salazar won re-election by a 20-point margin in 2024, but this year is facing a significant challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee and a former television news anchor. A poll conducted for his campaign late last month found him tied with Salazar. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.” First elected in 2020, the congresswoman is a champion of the Dignity Act, an immigration reform proposal in the House of Representatives that would create a pathway for some undocumented immigrants to obtain legal status. Salazar’s ad is the latest instance of Republican lawmakers seeking to put distance between themselves and Trump before the 3 Novembe

text: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak. The US health secretary added that he would’ve made sweeping changes ‘on day one’ but he had to follow the law. As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises, Robert F Kennedy Jr headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told anti-vaccine activists at the conference in a nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. He urged patience, saying that he would’ve made sweeping changes “on day one” but that he had to follow the law in order to make permanent change. “But as I said, you have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time,” Kennedy said. He only addressed the measles outbreak, which recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, once. “In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.” Recent polling suggests that one quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year in addition to those inPennsylvania. Kennedy described “vaccine-injured children” as “damaged” because of diagnoses of allergies, asthma, ADHD and autism, among other conditions. He also claimed that diabetes, sudden infant death syndrome, and anorexia can be side effects of routine vaccines, and he said that the system to track such effects is “broken”. There is little daylight between Kennedy and his former organization. “I spent 40 years in these battles,” Kennedy said. “I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able.” He thanked his friends

The extraordinary danger is that a president who believes he is the law, and the law is him, remains intent on disrupting the electoral process. For the millions of Americans who vote by mail – almost a third of the country – the week began with significant uncertainty that they would be able to easily submit their ballot this fall, thanks to a March executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to restrict mail-in ballots. By Monday night, the supreme court restored a measure of order by rebuking the president and rejecting his plan – but Trump’s frothing response portends more danger for the rapidly approaching midterms. text: No more book bans: how Florida students are pushing rightwingers out of school boards. Local communities are fighting back against the influence of conservative groups like Moms for Liberty in education. Jimmy Glover’s youngest children were in high school when he noticed their Florida school district taking an unsettling turn. Beloved books were being pulled from shelves. Teachers were scared of being targeted. “There was this culture of fear that was permeating throughout the district,” Glover said of Sarasota county. By channeling anger against mask mandates in schools, the rightwing group Moms for Liberty, founded in Florida, built an outsized influence on school boards across the country in 2022. Soon, members began pressuring schools to remake their curricula along conservative ideological lines, erasing mentions of LGBTQ+ Americans, slavery, racism and more. As a Black dad living in a historically Black part of Sarasota, Glover said he was especially disturbed by governor Ron DeSantis’s announcement that Florida schools would begin teaching students that some Black people benefited from slavery. “Now my children and the students in my community weren’t going to be learning about the true history of this country,” Glover said. So the father of four decided to run for Sarasota’s school board this year. He is part of a larger movement of students, parents, teachers and concerned community members pushing back against the influence of groups like Moms for Liberty in Florida public education. They wanted schools that were safe and welcoming for all students, and that focused on learning rather than scoring points on the national political scene. And last month, they won. A coalition of civil rights groups filed a lawsuit against Trump administration officials on Friday, seeking to stop them from threatening to deploy federal law enforcement officers to polling stations in the US midterm elections. Plaintiffs cited other examples of voter intimidation, such as Donald Trump giving a primetime address to exaggerate claims of noncitizen voting, the administration’s sweeping immigration enforcement operations in communities of color, and the president’s efforts to create a national voter eligibility list. Friday’s lawsuit is the latest attempt by groups to stop Trump from asserting more control over US elections as the country heads into what is expected to be a competitive midterm in November. text: MS Now, CNN and Politico say reporters have been denied access to White House. President said he was banning journalists from those organizations, saying of their coverage: ‘You get sick of it.’. Journalists from three US outlets were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning a day after Donald Trump said he would ban them from the executive branch complex in a move that has prompted outrage and shock from free-speech advocates. The outlets were television broadcasters MS Now and CNN as well as the political news website Politico. MS Now said a reporter and a cameraman had been denied access and had their White House press passes confiscated by the US Secret Service at a security gate outside the West Wing. CNN reported that its reporter Betsy Klein was also denied access and had her press pass seized too. Politico said White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett had received the same treatment. “The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS Now said, adding that it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our first amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy”. It said: “We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the president, the administration and the issues that impact the American people.” CNN said in a statement: “We have a right under the US constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.” Politico’s editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, said in a statement to the Politico newsroom: “We stand by [Haslett] and all reporters here covering the White House … We will vigorously defend our first amendment rights.” Trump’s threat to banish CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House has brought condemnation from first amendment advocates and Democratic officials, among others, as the conflict between the US president and parts of the media sharply escalates ahead of November’s midterm elections. It has also thrown into stark relief Trump’s attack on press freedom in the US

text: Leftists make waves and Trump flexes muscles: US primary season takeaways. Candidates have been selected for November’s midterms – have Republicans and Democrats made the right choices?. Primary season has officially concluded in the United States, with Democrats leading the polls among voters amid widespread economic anxieties, a war with Iran and Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda continuing into the end of the year. Democratic and Republican voters have selected contenders for key races in the 3 November midterms that will decide the balance of power in Congress, and the future of both parties. Democrats have been rocked by the primary victories of leftwing candidates. Republicans have doubled down on backing the president’s policies, despite his low approval ratings. And both parties are navigating the fallout from a series of scandals that have forced some candidates from the race, while others decided to press on. Here’s a look back at what we learned over the past six months of primaries: Lawmakers fled the House in droves, ensuring a reshaped Congress in 2027 Viewed as the chamber of Congress most likely to change hands in the midterms, the House saw significant turnover this cycle, with 74 members departing, the most since 1992, according to a tally from the Pew Research Center. Some outgoing lawmakers retired, while others ran for other offices, but generally didn’t fare particularly well – only 13 made it through primaries for governorships, the Senate or other offices, with the remaining 15 were rejected by voters. Among representatives who sought re-election to the House, 11 lost their primaries, the second-highest total since 2022. Coming midterm elections are starting to be framed not as right versus left but instead the ‘well-fed versus the fed-up’. Brian Leeland, a 79-year-old Democratic voter in Detroit, had enough. text: ‘I don’t trust him any more’: Pennsylvanians come to grips with John Fetterman’s rightwing turn. The maverick senator has isolated himself from supporters as he has become a strident supporter of Israel. Two eras, two videos, shot against the same physical backdrop, convey political messages that seem a world removed from each other. The contrasting films, produced eight years apart, neatly distill the evolution of John Fetterman, Pennsylvania’s maverick senator in his journey from progressive icon to a man seemingly more at ease with his nominal Republican opponents than his fellow Democrats. Fetterman’s evolution has been so stark that some Democrats fear he will go over to the Republicans – jeopardizing the party’s hopes of regaining control of the Senate – despite his disavowals of such intentions. Longtime activists say his stock within the party has dropped to the point where his chances of being re-elected as a Democrat are zero. A 2018 video for Fetterman’s successful campaign to be the state’s lieutenant governor opens with footage of Braddock, Pennsylvania’s landmark Mon Valley Edgar Thomson steelworks to the soundtrack of Donald Trump condemning previous US presidents for allowing industrial jobs to disappear and vowing that only he could bring them back. “Donald Trump hasn’t shown up since then, and he won’t because he never cared about places like this,” Fetterman says on camera, accusing Trump of using towns like Braddock as a prop. Braddock, a down-at-the-heel town of fewer than 2,000 residents on the Monongahela River near Pittsburgh, seemed emblematic of the left-behind communities Trump had wooed as he ran for president with promises to revive hollowed-out industries and restore lost jobs. It is also where Fetterman, a mayor for more than decade, cut his teeth as a highly unorthodox politician who broke with convention to attract investment to a shattered local economy and kickstart community projects, sometimes with his own money. María Elvira Salazar, the Republican congresswoman who has accused the president of going too far on immigration enforcement, doubled down on her criticism of the administration on Sunday, warning Donald Trump that some of his advisers were “compromising his legacy”. In an interview with CBS News’s Face the Nation, the Florida representative who is locked in a tight race for re-election pleaded with the US president not to “squander” his relationship with Hispanic voters. Though she couched her remarks as criticism of top administration advisers, it was clear that her focus was on Trump’s much-vaunted ambition to carry out the largest mass deportation of undocumented immigrants in US history. “I’m forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the south Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture,” she said. text: Whiplashed middle powers seek new alliances as Trump rages on world stage. While world leaders prepare for annual UN gathering, shifts in the global order continue in the face of a disruptive American president. In the event of a midterms election battering, it is possible that a deflated Donald Trump, constrained by a Democrat-controlled Congress, will gradually have to face up to the indignity of irrelevance. While continuing to sign off Truth Social posts with his usual, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, no one will actually be paying much attention. His meandering press conferences will no longer be carried live by TV networks. The Republican party will move on to the question of his successor. Trump could announce he had changed the name of the Champs-Élysées to Sunset Boulevard and even Google Maps will stifle a yawn. He would become that most pitied of political animals, the lame duck. Trump will also surely rage against the dying of the light. text: Monday briefing: Inside Trump’s deportation machine – ‘Your fate is out of your control’. In today’s newsletter: The US administration has built a system of removing migrants to countries they have no connection with, often with little warning. Good morning. If you want to grasp the true cost of what it means to “secure our borders,” skip the panicked headlines about “mega-dinghies” arriving on British shores and the pictures of Patriot Platform’s black-clad enthusiasts, and look across the Atlantic. Since 2025, the Trump administration has deported about 5,000 people on flights to “third countries” where they have no family ties or history, sometimes as far as Ghana and Sierra Leone. A Guardian investigation published today exposes the staggering cruelty of this sinister policy. It seems deliberately designed to stoke fear, and shows how far-right ideas that once belonged on the fringes of politics have become so mainstream that they’re now barely opposed. These deportations often happen very quickly, with people given little notice of what is going to happen to them. That creates huge challenges for lawyers trying to defend people who are shackled on flights, and for journalists trying to tell their stories. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s investigations correspondent Louisa Loveluck about the lives of the people caught up in this policy, and how the Trump administration has created a deportation machine. The larger question could re-emerge. Last week’s supreme court decision upholding the district court’s restraining order on USPS’s mail-in ballot restrictions is being hailed as a victory for electoral integrity by politicians, political commentators and voting rights advocates alike. The senator Chuck Schumer, for example, called the decision “one of the most important cases to protect voting rights before the supreme court”. But the unsigned, three-sentence opinion, with only a brief concurrence and a lengthy dissent, is no such thing. The court based its brief opinion entirely on the timing of the roll-out of the new rules, which became effective on 21 August, just weeks away from the midterm elections and only days before several states were scheduled to begin mailing out their ballots. text: Mark Carney is making an eloquent case for an alliance sidelining the US. The Canadian prime minister’s remarks before the European parliament outlined a vision of the west without its most powerful member. The speeches keep coming, each building on the previous one, as the Canadian prime minister builds a case for a new world order that has strikingly little to do with the United States of America, the country that has led the west since the second world war. On 20 January, in Davos, Mark Carney proposed that the world’s middle powers do more to support each other, in light of a “rupture” in the global order. That was clearly a reference to the destabilizing policies of Donald Trump, who had been inaugurated exactly one year earlier, and had spent most of that year insulting the US’s allies. On Thursday, before the European parliament in Strasbourg, Carney delivered another powerful oration that outlined what a new west might look like, without its most powerful member. In his speech, Carney signaled his desire to build bridges across the Atlantic at a time when the US-Canadian relationship is badly strained over trade disputes and Donald Trump’s kindergarten taunts. text: Trump and Mamdani appear friendly after ‘wide-ranging’ meeting at Gracie Mansion. Republican president said he hoped the democratic socialist would be a ‘great mayor’ for New York City. Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. At a news conference following their closed-door meeting at Gracie Mansion, Trump and Mamdani appeared friendly as they have in previous meetings. Mamdani said he and Trump held a “wide-ranging” discussion, which touched on affordable housing and immigration, but did not offer extensive details regarding any disagreements between them. Asked whether he challenged Trump over his decision to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from White House grounds, Mamdani said: “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in.” “It’s interesting because they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Trump chimed in, pointing to the large assembly of press on the lawn. The visit to Gracie Mansion, ahead of the president’s speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday, was a measure of Trump’s apparent respect for the 34-year-old mayor of his native New York. It was the first presidential visit to the historic riverside residence in 45 years, following Ronald Reagan, who met there with Ed Koch in 1981. Pressed on why he had invited Trump, Mamdani said he was willing to work with anybody who could “deliver” for New Yorkers, and highlighted their shared interest in building thousands of new housing units at Sunnyside Yard in Queens. For his part, Trump said he believed Mamdani had “great potential”. It was the latest unlikely meeting between Trump, a rightwing populist who has targeted immigrants and Muslims, and Mamdani, a democratic socialist who was born in Uganda and is New York’s first Muslim mayor. The Democratic Senate nominee’s views on Israel and comments after a synagogue attack prompted a public debate among Jewish voters. Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), was for about a decade a member of a rogue Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) group when he was in his late teens and 20s that some former members compared to a “cult”, according to a Guardian investigation. The Midtown group, which was based in the Washington DC area, attracted young people who were seeking help with addiction, sometimes at the urging of their parents. But while AA groups are traditionally a fellowship of people who come together to solve their drinking problem, former Midtown members say its one-time leader Michael Quinones – who died of cancer in 2007 – came to control nearly every aspect of their lives, including where they lived, worked and went to school. Trying to second-guess Donald Trump is a fool’s errand. So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. text: Another Florida Republican distances himself from Donald Trump before midterms. GOP nominee for governor Byron Donalds removes multiple mentions of president from his campaign website. Another prominent Florida Republican has publicly distanced himself from Donald Trump, days after María Elvira Salazar called out the US president’s immigration-enforcement policy targeting law-abiding undocumented immigrants. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor in November’s US midterm elections, launched an updated campaign website on Tuesday that was stripped of almost every mention of Trump and removed a photograph of the congressman and his wife, Erika, posing with the president, the Miami Herald reported. Until now, Donalds has proudly touted his close ties with the president, running a Republican primary campaign themed largely on Trump’s endorsement, and displaying a large banner on his website advertising his support. The move comes as Trump’s overall approval rating fell below 30% for the first time, dragged down by dissatisfaction over his handling of the US economy and the Iran war, and Republicans brace for heavy losses in November, including the possible loss of the party’s majorities in the US House of Representatives and Senate. On Tuesday, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, a top election prognosticator, moved the open Florida governor’s race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican”. “The GOP is still favored in both, but close polling, a bad political environment, and possible exhaustion with long periods of Republican leadership may make both of these races fairly close,” the report’s author, Kyle Kondik, wrote. The Herald’s reporting was based on research by the website tracking service Visualping, which recorded multiple changes to the Donalds site, including the removal of at least eight mentions of Trump from its homepage. Prior to the alterations, Donalds described himself as a “Trump-endorsed proven conservative fighter”, while other since-removed banners featured a “chip in to support Trump-endorsed Byron Donalds” fundraiser and one of Trump’s “run, Byron, run” endorsement announcements from last year. Iranian officials held three hours of talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Donald Trump disclosed on Tuesday. text: Full text: > I was 10 minutes into my first trip in a driverless car when I realised my vehicle was potentially obstructing the president of the United States. > Late for a press conference on the sidelines of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, I called one of the autonomous Waymos that I had seen gliding past my hotel. At first, the climate-controlled Jaguar purred serenely through the downtown traffic. Then, in the midst of a fast-flowing six-lane avenue, it came to an abrupt halt. The problem, it became apparent, was that police officers in the intersection ahead were diverting cars — with vigorous arm signals — to the right. My autonomous chauffeur was refusing to obey. > “Tell the Waymo it needs to go to the right,” bellowed the officer who stood in front of me. I was not sure to whom, or to what, I could communicate this, but sheepishly relayed his command out loud inside the car. There was no response. The Waymo kept pumping out soft jazz, indifferent to my appeals. > Unpanicked, I pressed the “call support” button on the display, assuming it would be answered in real time. The phone rang for what seemed like an eternity, with the officers in front of me growing more irate by the second. One further back suggested to her colleague that the Waymo was not budging because he was standing directly in front of it. He moved, but the car did not, presumably determined not to disobey the traffic lights, which had turned red. > By now, my Waymo was the lone civilian vehicle on the road and it dawned on me that the officers’ urgency might be due to the imminent arrival of a motorcade containing the convention’s headline act, Donald Trump, or a member of his cabinet. This was soon confirmed by the arrival of a Secret Service agent, wearing a black suit and a darker expression. “I need this vehicle to be out of here NOW, or it will be crushed,” he barked through the closed passenger window, strongly implying that I was somehow to blame. > At this point, the support line was answered by a distinctly unhurried voice who suggested moving everyone 10ft away from the perimeter of the car — a suggestion that the US Secret Service did not take kindly to. In any event, it made no difference. > I had seen enough. Against the advice of my remote interlocutor, I unbuckled my seatbelt, pushed the passenger door open, and fled into the 38C Dallas heat. Behind me, the agents continued to remonstrate with the recalcitrant vehicle. I looked back one last time to see the car, flanked by officers, finally start to crawl forward with its hazard lights on. > After making it to the conference centre, this time with an Uber under human control, I received a call from a Waymo representative. It was, they said, “not really the experience that we wanted you to have”. > The company’s press office later provided a more fulsome account of what went wrong. Apparently, the car had recognised and understood the officers’ hand gestures, but because the diversion required turning right across multiple lanes of traffic, it was programmed to wait for remote assistance. Said assistance was activated within seven seconds but was escalated to a team that deals with emergency personnel — hence the delay. > It’s not clear how often Waymo is involved in stand-offs with the Secret Service, but its safety record is significantly better than human drivers. The cars are active in more than 15 major US cities and, while it has filed over 1,000 incident reports with regulators, most of them are minor scrapes. > “We continually refine our technology’s performance to more seamlessly handle these types of scenarios,” a Waymo spokesperson said of my experience. “And we’ll continue to improve ahead of operating in environments where these situations are more common.” > Looking up Waymo’s expansion plans, I learnt one of its next targets is my home city, Washington DC, where impromptu diversions for passing VIPs are indeed “more common”. The company might want to consider fine-tuning its vehicles’ ability to navigate motorcades before they are deployed here.

The cars are active in more than 15 major US cities and, while it has filed over 1,000 incident reports with regulators, most of them are minor scrapes. > “We continually refine our technology’s performance to more seamlessly handle these types of scenarios,” a Waymo spokesperson said of my experience. “And we’ll continue to improve ahead of operating in environments where these situations are more common.” > Looking up Waymo’s expansion plans, I learnt one of its next targets is my home city, Washington DC, where impromptu diversions for passing VIPs are indeed “more common”. The company might want to consider fine-tuning its vehicles’ ability to navigate motorcades before they are deployed here.
