Republican senator calls bribery allegation ‘categorically false’ as ProPublica reports Trump derailed FBI inquiry. Democrats in Maine on Wednesday accused Republican senator Susan Collins of corruption after a major media outlet reported that the FBI had proposed investigating her for allegedly accepting bribes – before Donald Trump derailed the inquiry. The article from the investigative newsroom ProPublica rocked the race for Collins’s Senate seat, which is crucial to Democrats’ hopes of winning control of the chamber in the 3 November midterm election. The outlet reported that in the run-up to Collins’s successful bid for a fifth term in 2020, the head of her Super Pac had solicited a campaign donation from contracting firm Navatek, which demanded assurances of business from the government in return. Using a shell company, Navatek CEO Martin Kao later sent $150,000 to the Super Pac, then told other executives he had been informed Collins would ensure the firm won $32m in federal contracts. In late 2024, the FBI was moving towards investigating the arrangement, in what would have been a large-scale political bribery inquiry, but the agents leading the case were pushed out amid a wider purge of the bureau Trump ordered after returning to power last year, while a justice department office that oversees investigations of politicians was gutted. text: After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief. Locals hope agreement signed this week is step towards independence and end to US threats to annex island. Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief. Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over. To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath. text: EU says Trump’s plan to ban US diesel exports would ‘negatively impact both sides’. US president’s suggested 90-day export ban before midterm elections could bring even higher fuel prices across Europe. The EU has warned Donald Trump against plans to ban US diesel exports to the global market, saying the move would negatively affect Europe and the US. The European Commission has reacted with “concern” to reports this week that the US president could prevent diesel from reaching the global market. Trump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban to provide a temporary respite from high pump prices for US households before the midterm elections, after US diesel reached a record average of $6.52 (£4.93) a gallon. “I’ve said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” he said. Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the EU’s executive arm, said on Thursday “any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides” and the EU expected “close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets”. The EU made the diplomatic intervention as experts said that the potential export ban could be “devastating” for Europe, and traders scrambled to assess the continent’s reliance on imports from the US. The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has warned at an Economist event in New York that banning exports was a “blunt tool” that could harm US fuel supplies in the long term. For Europe, the ban could be far more damaging. US diesel exports have made up a third of the continent’s imports this year, as supplies from war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia have plummeted. text: US mortgage rates top 7% for first time in 20 months. Increase comes after Fed decision to raise interest rates, as Americans struggle with high prices and stagnant wages. US mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac, aggravating a housing market that has endured years of high interest rates and low supply. The increase comes after the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates, which directly affect mortgage rates, for the first time since 2023, citing high inflation. Rates on 16 September went up by a quarter of a point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year. Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023. But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran. The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday. On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month. Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise. The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com, with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year. “A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith. High mortgage rates are just one of the many reasons why Americans are struggling to attain home ownership.

In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year. Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023. But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran. The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday. On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month. Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise. The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com, with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year. “A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith. text: Iran war drives UK diesel price to near record high, and makes interest rate rise ‘hard to avoid’ – as it happened . Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey says persistently high oil and gas prices would make it hard to resist pressure to raise interest rates. We started the day with the news that UK consumer confidence has picked up, but it’s a different story in the US. ﻿Consumer sentiment across the US ticked down to a four month low in September, according to the University of Michigan’s regular index. Their index of consumer sentiment dropped to 48.1 this month, down from 51.7 in August. That’s 12% lower than a year ago. Worryingly for Donald Trump’s party, Republican sentiment is now 20% lower than January 2026; Democrats are down 13% over the same period. Surveys of Consumers director Joanne Hsu explains: Views of current and year-ahead expected personal finances both weakened about 10% this month, with concerns over high prices continuing to climb. Buying conditions for durables improved a bit, in part due to a perception that completing such purchases now would help consumers avoid higher prices in the future. The short-run outlook for business conditions plunged amid renewed worries that elevated fuel prices and re-escalating trade disputes could pass through to the economy as a whole. Overall, interviews reveal broad agreement across the political spectrum that the outlook for the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year. Time to wrap up… UK diesel drivers have been warned to expect record costs at the pumps within days. The average price of a litre of diesel has risen to 198.32p a litre today, near to the previous record of just over 199p a litre, set in 2022. The Trump administration is removing 760,000 people enrolled in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace on allegations of fraud, officials said on Tuesday – adding to previous efforts to chip away at federally subsidized insurance programs and likely causing some of the lowest-income Americans to forego healthcare, experts said. The US government is also investigating about 420,000 people whom they suspect of fraud, and they are putting a six-month enrollment moratorium on new agents and brokers selling Obamacare policies, officials said at a press conference. The removed enrollees are a mixture of “phantoms” and “ghosts” as well as people who don’t meet the eligibility requirements of Obamacare, said Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). “These are not real people,” he said, claiming that expelling them from the ACA marketplace would save the federal government $2.2bn. text: New Jersey lieutenant governor resigns after sexual harassment accusation. Investigation determined Dale Caldwell violated state ethics rules and engaged in harassing behavior. Dale Caldwell, the lieutenant governor of New Jersey, resigned from his position on Friday, after the release of a report accusing him of sexually harassing a female staffer, among other ethics violations. New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill, announced on Friday afternoon that Caldwell had submitted his resignation to her earlier in the day. The decision by Caldwell, 66, came one day after Sherrill called on him to step down after an investigation determined he violated state ethics rules and engaged in behavior that constituted sexual harassment. The 61-page report said it found credible evidence that Caldwell made romantic advances toward a female staffer’s friend, tried to secure a promotion for his girlfriend and gave tickets to personal guests without reimbursement. The New Jersey Globe was the first to report on Caldwell’s resignation. text: My human summarization of the decision: - SAVE was a database established in 1986 to determine if immigrants were eligible for federal benefits - Starting in 2005, some states used it to check their voter registrations - By executive order, the administration merged it with the SSN database to make bulk searches easier - Organizations sued, and a lower court said the administration had to hold off on rolling out the changes while the lawsuit was pending. The Supreme Court overruled the stay, saying the lawsuit had not proved enough merit to stop the policy while the lawsuits proceed. - It is still up to states whether they use SAVE or not. If someone shows up in the SAVE database, the state may ask them to provide proof of citizenship. The concern here from the dissent is that states are going to purge their voter registrations while awaiting the ruling. But realistically, the states interested in doing this don't have enough time before midterms to do this - as they would have to then process all of the proof-of-citizenship documentation or open themselves up to mass lawsuits. Update: Per NPR, the SAVE database covers 65 million voters in 26 states, of which 28,635 have been flagged as "potential noncitizens". https://www.opb.org/article/2026/09/25/the-supreme-court-rev... In Texas, using this dataset, they were only able to bring forward 117 cases of fraudulent voting.

text: Nearly 200 people wrongly identified on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens. State election officials said they reviewed 185 records homeland security sent them and confirmed they were US citizens. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) wrongly identified 185 people on Nevada’s voter rolls as non-citizens, state officials said this week, escalating concerns over the shoddy methodology the government is using to raise fear about non-citizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. In July, Donald Trump gave a speech saying DHS had found a combined 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls in Nevada, California, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Follow-up letters to each of those states weakened the claim, saying there only could be as many as 278,000 non-citizens on the rolls, including up to 15,903 in Nevada. In August, DHS officials told staffers in the Nevada secretary of state’s office that they had reviewed the numbers and confirmed only 185 were non-citizens. DHS officials said they still needed to review more than 14,000 records. But on Wednesday, Nevada election officials said they had reviewed the 185 records DHS sent them and confirmed they were US citizens. “As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens. You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise,” Greg Ott, a deputy attorney general, wrote to DHS this week in an email obtained by the Guardian through a public records request. The message was first reported by the New York Times and Nevada Independent. In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson did not address whether the department still believed the 185 were non-citizens. The spokesperson said the agency “is providing a service to the citizens of Nevada”. “The list of 185 were simply a subset of individuals that had gone through a rigorous manual review process at that time of the call. The list shared with Nevada last month also included 6,218 individuals with the highest number of matching attributes to an alien in DHS records,” the spokesperson said. In his email, Ott lamented DHS had not been transparent about the methodology DHS had used to flag alleged non-citizens nor had it shared adequate information. When

In a lengthy statement sent to news outlets, the White House press office insisted that versions of the ad, which feature audio of Trump urging voters to help him “defeat communism” and a whirlwind video review of his second term, were simply routine “public service announcements” like those produced by previous administrations. However, while the Trump administration ad features the president in almost every frame, and includes words of praise for him offered by a prominent supporter during the 2024 campaign, none of the advertising from three prior administrations the White House called similar featured any partisan messaging or showed images of Trump’s predecessors. text: Trump allies could use midterms ‘counting window’ to disrupt results, experts warn. Fears grow that loyalists in key states could use critical period when votes are counted to amplify false claims. Election experts have warned Donald Trump’s administration could use the crucial hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce a crackdown on voting. With less than six weeks remaining until polls close, and control of US Congress in the balance, the post-election “counting window” is seen as as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials. text: Saturday Night Live: Jalen Brunson makes for stiff host in underwhelming season premiere. There are some promising moments from newer cast members, but the show’s return, after a politically tumultuous period, was lacking in bite. The 52nd season of Saturday Night Live opens inside the New York City mayor’s office. Mayor Zohran Mamdani (Ramy Youssef, reprising the role from last season) gets a surprise visit from Donald Trump (James Austin Johnson). The president, who “for some reason that no one can figure out” loves Mamdani, has braved the big El Niño storm to visit his “day one”. Trump unloads about his busy week – banning members of the press from the White House pool, delivering apocalyptic threats to Iran at the UN, consulting with AI leaders including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg (“It made me think, wow, RFK Jr’s probably right about those vaccines, I mean, the ‘tizz in that room …”) – before being interrupted by his assistant Natalie Harp (Ashley Padilla). Acting like “the girl from Obsession, but blond”, the dangerously jealous Harp threatens Mamdani. Trump eventually convinces the mayor to let him stay and hang out in New York in exchange for $20bn for a housing project in Queens. A rather weak cold open considering it’s the season premiere. Padilla’s caricature of Harp as a deranged, Fatal Attraction-like stalker is gold and should have been the focus here. text: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war. Waltz says Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to end war because they ‘were asking for everything up front’. The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”. Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz. “They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.” Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said. Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”. In comments to Axios on Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.” Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace. Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”. Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel.

text: - The Trump administration is releasing more oil from the nation’s emergency reserve as fuel prices surge less than two months before the midterm elections. - The offer of up to 40 million barrels represents the last of a 172-million-barrel emergency drawdown from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve ordered to tame soaring energy prices after the US invasion of Iran. Bids are due by 11:00 a.m. central time on October 6, according to a statement from the Department of Energy. - The SPR is projected to fall to its lowest level since 1982 once the latest release is completed. Federal law bars non-emergency drawdowns once inventories fall below 252.4 million barrels, while a 1981 report from the US Government Accountability Office advised against releases below 250 million barrels except in a “very severe emergency.” The reserve’s operational minimum — the point at which it becomes difficult for the infrastructure to function — is around 70 million barrels, according to ClearView Energy Partners, a Washington-based consulting firm.

Republicans supported legislation although Democrats said it wouldn’t effectively address energy consumption. Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation intended to offset the impact of datacenters on consumer electricity bills, calling it a “toothless” attempt to address a top voter concern ahead of November’s midterm elections. text: Senate blocks Republican bill restricting stock trades by US Congress members. Democrats block measure they say didn’t go far enough – and was bundled with ‘poison pill’ voter ID rules. The US Senate on Wednesday blocked a Republican bill restricting stock trading by members of Congress, after Democrats refused to advance a measure they said would let lawmakers keep their portfolios and was bundled with voter ID rules they called a “poison pill”. The 53-47 vote fell seven short of the 60 needed to open debate on the Stop Insider Trading Act, which the Republican-controlled House passed in July. Every Democrat and independent voted no, and the failure comes five weeks before the 3 November midterms. The bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses and their dependent children from buying individual stocks. Democrats said that falls short of a ban because lawmakers could keep everything they already own, reinvest dividends into more shares and let a spouse or child trade on their behalf. Several also wanted the rules extended to the president and other White House officials, while others objected to the photo ID requirements for voting, which they said would make it harder for eligible citizens to cast ballots. Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, called the bill “a permission slip for corruption” and said Republicans had designed it to fail. He noted that a Senate committee advanced a bipartisan ban last year and accused Republicans of ignoring it. His deputy, Dick Durbin, dismissed the “meaningless” bill as “an inadequate congressional stock trading ban” and “Republican messaging”. Republicans said Democrats had picked politics over reform. Nebraska’s Pete Ricketts, who faces a tight re-election race, said on the Senate floor “we need to restore the faith of the American people” in Congress. Joe Gruters, chair of the Republican National Committee, accused Democrats of choosing to “protect the swamp” over voter ID and accountability and said “voters should hold them accountable in November”. Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel. Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban. The warning marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential wider ban to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November. Trump said Washington could ask its European allies to release strategic diesel reserves. “We may do that. They have some diesel,” Trump told reporters on a midterm elections campaign trip to Texas, shortly after the Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, urged Europe to “immediately” release its reserves. Bessent flagged the potential diesel cuts in a social media post, writing: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.” Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday. The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks. text: The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped. These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives. A turning point in Donald Trump’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority. Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration. These charts and maps reveal where the battle for Congress will be fought. Polling shows there has been a nationwide shift towards the Democrats in the run-up to the midterms, even in states Republicans have dominated for decades. Many recent surveys of the generic ballot, a key indicator of voters’ intent in congressional elections, give the Democrats an edge ranging from the high single digits to the low double digits. The events of this year – notably the Iran war and its impact on inflation – have undoubtedly changed the race, and much of the advantage seems to have swung towards the Democrats. Across all key races, Democratic candidates have been campaigning on affordability, at a time when the Trump administration’s actions in the Middle East have pushed up prices, particularly for gasoline and diesel. It is a reflection of just how concerned US voters are about the economy, rating it as the most important issue in surveys, far ahead of immigration, healthcare or civil rights. Meanwhile, Trump’s personal ratings have also fallen, with Reuters/Ipsos finding only 32% of US adults now approve of his job performance. That is worse than his previous low of 34%, recorded by Gallup at the end of his first term in 2021 after the January 6 attack on the US Capitol. The 2026 midterms may be another brutal reckoning for the US president – the question is whether punishment from voters will lead him to change course.

But in July, heavy machinery gouged the earth where mesquite and dense brush once grew. A steel barricade of 30ft-high bars was erected across the riverfront, including on his property just across the Rio Grande from Mexico. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added. Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years. US economy only added 29,000 jobs in September, which might deter the Federal Reserve from raising interest rates. Time to wrap up…. US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election. The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of just under 70,000 new jobs. Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. text: Hundreds gather in Mississippi to protest Republican redistricting: ‘This fight is familiar territory’. Dozens of residents testify to legislature’s redistricting committee in heated hearing, the last of eight. Hundreds of people gathered across from the Mississippi state capitol building on Thursday evening to rally against the aggressive Republican efforts to draw maps that favor their own party. text: The Tejano singer trying to win back Latinos who voted for Trump, one quinceañera at a time. Bobby Pulido has a strategy: show up at the 15th birthday parties that are a rite of passage in the Texas borderlands – and flip a key House district for Democrats. It took all of two minutes for Bobby Pulido’s electoral stealth weapon to come into play. The Tejano music star turned Democratic congressional candidate had barely begun canvassing in the high school football stadium in Edinburg, Texas, when a 15-year-old girl came rushing up to him. “Señor Pulido! Señor Pulido!” she cried. The 85-mile dash to Oklahoma at nearly 100mph was proof that nothing can keep Trump from a Trump rally. Which might not be the good news for Republicans it once was. Trump’s approval rating is at an all-time low. Voters are angry about the cost of living, the Iran war and excessive immigration crackdowns. Considered a radical and even fringe idea for decades, interest in sweeping healthcare reform has surged as progressive Democrats have won a series of primary victories before November’s crucial midterm elections. Los Angeles is a deeply blue city and the mayor’s race has become a bitter battle between two progressives who have come to represent the clashing wings of the Democratic party. text: > using their own brains Nonsense. There's no "using your own brains" in voting in the midterms. You get no information about the vast majority of the candidates, you're just expected to vote as the party tells you to, and the rest of the information you get is from PR firms in proportion to the millions spent to market to you and distort all the information that you could possibly find. Even if you work your hardest and get a reasonable overview, you've dedicated far more of your time to this than anyone could be expected to (a sign of the leisure and access you have as a privileged middle-class person), and the vote will be necessarily decided by the vast majority who didn't. People using LLMs for the midterms will be the best informed voters we've had in a long time, even if they use Grok (which will desperately try to lie to them, and won't be the only one.) They should also use LLMs to help them with strategies to get to an actual voting booth, because the parties like to sabotage voting in places they feel they'll be weak. You seem to think everybody (but you) is a dummy and will just do what the LLM says to do, but were totally comfortable for them just doing what the party says to do. I might use an LLM myself to figure out what's going on with judges, if I can find one with access to the proper databases. In fact, if you want to do good for the world, get access to good databases with good search engines, hook deepseek up to them, and open it to the public. People need to find out how judges decide, and if there are any complaints against them, etc.

Hilton faces heavy backlash from within his own party for ‘Just Try It’ ad amid his longshot bid for California governor. Steve Hilton, the Republican candidate for California governor, is receiving heavy criticism from members of his own party over a controversial, sexual innuendo-filled campaign ad that has been described as “creepy”. The video entitled “Just Try It, California” was released last week and depicts two young women with brightly colored hair, sitting on a bed in front of a pride flag in low lighting. One nervously says “I can’t believe I’m doing this”, while another strokes her hair and coaxes “don’t be nervous, it’s not that bad” before guiding her to fill out a ballot for Hilton and aggressively commanding “lick it”. The controversy comes as Hilton, a British former political adviser to David Cameron and Fox News host, is fighting to advance his longshot bid against Xavier Becerra, the former health secretary. With just a few weeks to go before the November midterm elections, Hilton is trailing in the polls. Sonja Shaw, the Republican nominee for California superintendent of public instruction, called the new campaign ad “creepy, weird, disturbing garbage”. “This is a clear example of exactly why good people are walking away from the Republican party. As a mother and someone who has fought to protect the innocence of children, this crosses a line. We have lost our way,” she wrote on social media. Michael Gates, the party’s nominee for state attorney general, also condemned the advertisement, stating that he “emphatically [denounced] the use of young women as a political tool”. Hilton faces tough odds in the deep blue state, where voters haven’t elected a Republican to lead since 2004. Polls have consistently shown Becerra with a significant lead over Hilton. Hilton is trying to rally California’s Republicans while converting Democrats and independents frustrated with the ever-increasing cost of living in California. text: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show. President says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 voters. Donald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%. That polling included the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip could prove dire for the Republican party a month before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Before boarding a flight to Nebraska on Monday, Trump shrugged off questions about his approval ratings. “I’m doing great,” Trump told a reporter, who had asked about recent polls showing the president losing support among Latino voters, before blaming CNN and the media. But according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll release Sunday, 59% of Latino voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress, double the number that supported the party two years ago. According to that poll, just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance. Trump has spent the past few days campaigning across the country for Republican candidates, despite even conservative states starting to show the loss of support. Some Republicans have also started to distance themselves from the president over issues such as immigration as they attempt to hold on to local support. With Americans souring on the economy, the war with Iran, and other key issues they attribute to the administration, the impact of the negative sentiments could reach far and wide.
